prompt: What keeps hundreds of sites on one shared machine apart from each other?
hint: You met the mechanism in lesson six.

choices.text: The `Host` header, which names the site the request is for
choices.why: One line of text turned one address into as many sites as anybody wanted.

choices.text: A separate process for each site, started when a request for it arrives
choices.why: Processes may be shared or separate, and neither is what routes the request.

choices.text: The certificate presented, which the server uses to pick the right folder
choices.why: The name in the certificate is checked by the browser, not used for routing.

choices.text: A separate address for each account, assigned by the provider
choices.why: One address serves them all, which is why addresses stopped running out.

prompt: A site on shared hosting becomes popular and starts returning errors while the machine sits idle. What happened?
hint: The tell is an error at a consistent number rather than a gradual slowdown.

choices.text: The machine ran out of memory and the site's process was killed
choices.why: That shows as the machine being busy rather than idle.

choices.text: A per-account limit was reached
choices.why: Many panels count processes or connections, and cut off rather than slow down.

choices.text: A neighbour is using the processor, so requests queue until they time out
choices.why: That is the noisy neighbour, and it makes things slow rather than refused.

choices.text: The provider's firewall treated the traffic as an attack and dropped it
choices.why: Possible on a real flood, and it would not coincide with a fixed number of visitors.

prompt: Fill the blank: on shared hosting the processor, the memory and the ___ are shared, so a neighbour who sends spam attaches a reputation to your mail as well.
hint: It is the thing DNS resolves to.

prompt: Which of these are signals that it is time to leave shared hosting? Choose all that apply.
hint: Each is about a limit rather than about ambition.

choices.text: You need a language version or a background worker the panel does not offer
choices.why: Specific, and you will recognise it.

choices.text: You hit an account limit rather than the machine's capacity
choices.why: An error at a consistent number of visitors is the tell.

choices.text: You need to deploy from a repository, repeatably, with a way back
choices.why: Panels that expect uploads by hand make that possible and unpleasant.

choices.text: Your site has become important to you
choices.why: The most common reason people give, and not a signal about anything.

choices.text: You want the site to be faster than a shared machine can be
choices.why: For a site of content the machine is rarely what is slow.

prompt: Why is uploading files by hand a problem beyond being tedious?
hint: Ask what you can recover, and what two people can agree on.

choices.text: The panel compresses uploads, so large files arrive damaged now and then
choices.why: Nothing damages them; the objection is about history rather than integrity.

choices.text: It is slower than a repository, which matters when a site has many files
choices.why: True and trivial beside what is actually lost.

choices.text: There is no record of what changed and no way back to yesterday
choices.why: The site becomes whatever the last person uploaded.

choices.text: Files uploaded that way arrive with permissions the web server refuses
choices.why: A real annoyance, fixed once, and unrelated to the deeper cost.

prompt: What is the word *private* doing in *virtual private server*?
hint: It is about what a neighbour can take.

choices.text: It means the traffic to it is encrypted by the provider before it leaves
choices.why: Nothing about the name concerns encryption.

choices.text: It means the address is unpublished, so nobody else knows it
choices.why: The address is public like any other; it has to be reachable.

choices.text: It means the machine is kept for you and shared with nobody
choices.why: It is shared; the slicing is what makes the sharing bearable.

choices.text: It means the allocation of processor, memory and disk is yours
choices.why: A neighbour's load does not take it, which is the whole difference.

prompt: A new machine goes up with a password login and no updates applied. How long before it is found?
hint: The logs of any new server answer this.

choices.text: Hours
choices.why: Automated scanning finds public addresses continuously, and that is not an exaggeration.

choices.text: Weeks, and just if the address appears in a public record somewhere
choices.why: Nothing has to publish it; the whole space is scanned.

choices.text: Months, unless a name is pointed at it and the name is indexed
choices.why: Scanning works on addresses and has no interest in names.

choices.text: It depends on the provider, since some filter scanning before it arrives
choices.why: Some filter a little, and nothing you would rely on.

prompt: Fill the blank: when a machine runs out of ___, the system kills the largest process — which is your application or your database — so the site goes down rather than slowing down.
hint: Not the disk and not the processor.

prompt: Why is a full disk worse than it sounds?
hint: Ask what can still be written.

choices.text: The site slows to the speed of whatever free space remains
choices.why: There is no slower mode; writes fail rather than degrade.

choices.text: Writes fail, including the log entry that would tell you why
choices.why: And often the session that would let you log in to fix it.

choices.text: The provider suspends the machine until space is freed from their side
choices.why: Providers do not police your disk usage inside your own allocation.

choices.text: The database refuses reads as well, since it writes a temporary file per query
choices.why: Some queries do use temporary space, and reads are not generally refused.

prompt: What makes a server you control genuinely different from one you were given?
hint: Something you can do to it that shared hosting never allows.

choices.text: The provider monitors the application and restarts it when it stops
choices.why: Their responsibility ends at the hardware and the network.

choices.text: The traffic is faster, since there are no neighbours competing for the network
choices.why: Network capacity is usually not the constraint, and it is not the difference.

choices.text: It is rebuilt from a file in a repository
choices.why: Which turns a server from something you fear into something you can throw away.

choices.text: Backups are taken automatically, which shared hosting does not offer
choices.why: Backwards: shared hosts often take them and on your own machine it is your job.

prompt: Match each layer to what stops being yours.
hint: Read them as positions on one line.

pairs.right: Nothing above the hardware: the system and the runtime are yours
The operating system and the runtime, which the provider now runs
Everything but one piece of code, and nothing runs between calls

right_distractors: The application itself, which the provider writes
The data, which the provider takes responsibility for

prompt: What is the actual innovation of renting machines by the hour?
hint: It is about what you can undo.

choices.text: The provider takes responsibility for the software running on them
choices.why: At the lowest layer they take responsibility for nothing above the hardware.

choices.text: The cost is lower than owning hardware over the life of the machine
choices.why: Often higher, and the argument was never really about the total.

choices.text: The machines usually run faster than the ones a company buys for itself
choices.why: Often the opposite, and speed is not what changed.

choices.text: Capacity became a decision you change on the day you need to
choices.why: And it is why a company can survive being on the news.

prompt: Fill the blank: before writing any code against an hourly-priced provider, set a ___ alarm — ten minutes that turn a catastrophe into a message.
hint: It is about money.

prompt: A service handles steady, constant traffic. Why are functions a poor fit?
hint: Compare with the thing they replace.

choices.text: A small server is cheaper and simpler for load that never stops
choices.why: Nothing runs between calls is worth nothing when there is always a call.

choices.text: They cannot be placed behind a load balancer, so traffic cannot be spread
choices.why: Spreading is what the provider does with them by default.

choices.text: Their cold start applies to every call rather than to the first
choices.why: Backwards: constant traffic is what keeps them warm.

choices.text: They are limited to short executions, so a steady service would be cut off
choices.why: Limits exist and are generous; steadiness is not what trips them.

prompt: Which piece of a cloud setup is easiest to move to another provider?
hint: Ask what would have to be rewritten.

choices.text: The provider's functions, which are ordinary code with a wrapper
choices.why: The wrapper is the architecture, and moving means rewriting.

choices.text: A machine running your own software
choices.why: The same configuration builds the same thing elsewhere in an afternoon.

choices.text: A managed database, since the data exports in a standard format
choices.why: Portable with effort: the data comes out and the arrangements are rebuilt.

choices.text: A platform's build system, which follows the same conventions everywhere
choices.why: Conventions differ, and this is one of the deeper commitments.

prompt: What happens to a static site under a sudden surge of visitors?
hint: Ask what work each request costs.

choices.text: It depends on the generator, since pages are produced as they are requested
choices.why: The generator ran at build time; nothing is produced during a visit.

choices.text: It slows down in proportion, as the file server queues the requests
choices.why: Serving a file is the cheapest thing a computer does; queuing is unlikely.

choices.text: It costs a little more bandwidth
choices.why: A different relationship with popularity than anything else in the lesson.

choices.text: It falls over at the point where the connections exceed what one machine holds
choices.why: That point is far higher than for anything that runs code per request.

prompt: Somebody objects that a real site changes and cannot be static. What is the answer?
hint: The distinction is about when, not whether.

choices.text: Content changes are held until a weekly publication, which suits most sites
choices.why: Nothing requires a schedule; a build runs whenever you like.

choices.text: The objection holds, and static hosting suits documentation alone
choices.why: It stretches much further, which is what surprises people.

choices.text: Static sites are rebuilt by the browser on each visit, so they are current
choices.why: Nothing is rebuilt in a browser; the file is what it is.

choices.text: The pages are assembled in advance and rebuilt when the content changes
choices.why: Publish an article, rebuild in seconds, and the visitor still receives a file.

prompt: Fill the blank: the service that holds files by the gigabyte, in buckets, with no machine involved, is called ___ storage.
hint: It stores things with a name and some metadata.

prompt: Which of these mean a site cannot be files alone? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four recognisable cases.

choices.text: The page differs per visitor — a dashboard or a basket
choices.why: Something has to assemble that, on a server or after a call from the browser.

choices.text: The content changes faster than a rebuild can run
choices.why: A build of a minute is fine for a blog and useless for a moving price.

choices.text: Something must happen on receipt — a payment, an email, a record written
choices.why: That is a call to something else, and the something else is small.

choices.text: The site has more than a few hundred pages
choices.why: Generators produce thousands; the limit is build time and it is far off.

choices.text: The site needs a search box
choices.why: A search box is a call from the page to a service, and the page stays a file.

prompt: What is the most common serious mistake made with object storage?
hint: It is a setting rather than a bug.

choices.text: A bucket left readable by everybody
choices.why: Every provider warns loudly, and it keeps happening.

choices.text: Treating it as a disk and relying on folders that do not really exist
choices.why: A real confusion, and an inconvenience rather than a disclosure.

choices.text: Storing a database in it, which is slow and expensive to query
choices.why: A poor idea and one people rarely attempt.

choices.text: Uploading files that are larger than the practical limit for a single object
choices.why: The limits are enormous and are not where the damage comes from.

prompt: A page takes two seconds to build on the server. What does putting a CDN in front do for it?
hint: Separate the two numbers from lesson three.

choices.text: It halves the time, since the edge does part of the work closer to the visitor
choices.why: An edge performs none of your work; it holds copies of results.

choices.text: It still takes two seconds to build
choices.why: A CDN is a distance fix rather than a speed fix.

choices.text: It makes the page faster once the edge has cached it, and not before
choices.why: Close, and it is about cacheability rather than about the build time.

choices.text: It makes it slower, because each request now passes through an extra machine
choices.why: True for uncached requests, and the two seconds are the point here.

prompt: What happens the first time somebody in a region asks an edge for a file it does not have?
hint: Once per edge.

choices.text: The file is copied to each edge at once, so the next region pays no fetch
choices.why: That is the push arrangement, and it is not how a pull network behaves.

choices.text: The edge waits for a scheduled synchronisation with the origin
choices.why: There is no schedule; the fetch happens because somebody asked.

choices.text: The edge fetches it from your server, keeps a copy, and answers
choices.why: Every visitor after that is served locally.

choices.text: The request is refused and the browser is sent to the origin instead
choices.why: Nothing sends the visitor elsewhere; the edge fetches on their behalf.

prompt: Fill the blank: the word for your own server, the thing behind the edges, is the ___.
hint: It appears in every provider’s settings.

prompt: A signed-in dashboard is served through a CDN with no caching instruction. What is the risk?
hint: It is the failure from lesson seven at a larger scale.

choices.text: The session cookie is stripped, since edges drop headers they do not know
choices.why: Edges pass cookies through; stripping them would break each site behind one.

choices.text: The edge holds the page until its own default expiry, which browsers disregard
choices.why: Browsers honour what they are told, and the holding is not the danger here.

choices.text: The page is slower, because the edge is no help with a personalised request
choices.why: True, and it is the cost rather than the risk.

choices.text: One visitor's page is stored and served to the next
choices.why: A shared cache, now distributed across a hundred countries.

prompt: Which of these does a CDN genuinely help with? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the five are about something it never touches.

choices.text: The distance between a visitor and a cached file
choices.why: Two hundred milliseconds becoming ten.

choices.text: The load on your own server
choices.why: It drops to whatever the edges could not answer.

choices.text: Surviving a flood aimed at your site
choices.why: A few hundred machines with enormous capacity instead of your one.

choices.text: A slow database query behind a page
choices.why: It holds copies of results and has no opinion about producing them.

choices.text: A page that loads four megabytes of script
choices.why: The script arrives faster and is still four megabytes to execute.

prompt: Why are free certificates issued with a short validity?
hint: It forces something.

choices.text: It forces the renewal to be automated
choices.why: Nothing lasts long enough to survive on somebody remembering.

choices.text: Because browsers refuse certificates valid for longer than a year
choices.why: Browsers do cap validity, and that is not why the free ones are short.

choices.text: So that a compromised key is useful for a shorter period
choices.why: A genuine benefit, and not the reason the model is built this way.

choices.text: Because a shorter certificate is cheaper for the authority to sign
choices.why: The signing cost is the same whatever the dates say.

prompt: A site redirects all plain HTTP to HTTPS and certificate renewal stops working. What is the likely cause?
hint: One of the two ways of proving control needs something you just redirected.

choices.text: The authority requires a wildcard once HTTPS is enforced sitewide
choices.why: Wildcards are about covering subdomains and are unrelated to this.

choices.text: The authority asks for a file over plain HTTP, and the redirect answers instead
choices.why: Which is why *we redirected everything* is a common and confusing failure.

choices.text: The certificate is refused while the old one is still valid
choices.why: Renewal happens well before expiry by design.

choices.text: The redirect changes the name being requested, so the challenge is for the wrong one
choices.why: A redirect to HTTPS keeps the name; the scheme is what changed.

prompt: Fill the blank: obtaining a ___ certificate, which covers every subdomain at once, requires proving control through DNS rather than over HTTP.
hint: It has a star in it.

prompt: A site works on your laptop and shows a certificate warning on somebody’s phone. What is the usual cause?
hint: Something the server should have sent and did not.

choices.text: The certificate covers the `www` name and the phone asked for the bare one
choices.why: A real fault, and it would fail on your laptop in exactly the same way.

choices.text: The phone’s clock is wrong, so the certificate looks as if it has not started
choices.why: It happens, and it would not correlate with the device the way this does.

choices.text: The chain is incomplete, and your browser had the missing piece already
choices.why: The worst way for this to present: it works where you are looking.

choices.text: The phone refuses the cipher the server offered, and reports it as a certificate fault
choices.why: That produces a connection error rather than a certificate warning.

prompt: What should a certificate alert be based on?
hint: Failure is not the signal you want.

choices.text: The browser warning, since that is what a visitor would see
choices.why: That is the outage, which is the thing being avoided.

choices.text: The authority’s notification email, which arrives before expiry
choices.why: It may arrive, to an address that may be read.

choices.text: The renewal failing, which is the moment something has gone wrong
choices.why: By then there may be weeks left, and nothing is looking during them.

choices.text: The number of days remaining
choices.why: A failure has weeks in which it could be fixed, and nobody looks during them.

prompt: A restaurant wants five pages and a contact form, updated twice a year. What fits?
hint: Ask how much of a machine needs to be anybody’s problem.

choices.text: Static hosting, with the form submitting to a small service
choices.why: Nothing to patch, nothing to back up, and popularity costs bandwidth.

choices.text: Shared hosting with a content system, so staff can edit the pages
choices.why: Defensible, and it takes on an application to keep updated for two edits a year.

choices.text: Functions, since the traffic is occasional and idle time is free
choices.why: Fine for the form, and no way to serve five pages from it.

choices.text: A virtual server, so the form can be handled by an application you control
choices.why: A machine to patch, for a form that submits twice a week.

prompt: An application needs a background worker, a scheduled job and a specific language version. What does that rule out?
hint: One option offers none of the three.

choices.text: Static hosting, which has no way to run code of any kind
choices.why: True and obvious, and it was never a candidate for an application.

choices.text: Shared hosting
choices.why: The panel exposes what it exposes, and none of those is usually on the list.

choices.text: Functions, which have no way to run anything on a schedule
choices.why: Scheduled invocation is a standard feature of every functions product.

choices.text: A platform, which runs one process and refuses anything beside it
choices.why: Most platforms run workers and scheduled jobs as first-class things.

prompt: A service is idle most of the week and receives ten thousand requests in one hour each Friday. What suits it?
hint: Nothing runs between calls.

choices.text: A platform with one small instance, scaled by hand before each Friday
choices.why: Workable, and it is a person doing what the previous option does by itself.

choices.text: A virtual server sized for the Friday peak, which is simple to reason about
choices.why: You pay for the peak all week, which is the argument against it.

choices.text: Functions
choices.why: Nothing is paid for between calls, and the burst is the provider's problem.

choices.text: Shared hosting, since the weekly average is small
choices.why: The average is small and the hour would meet every account limit at once.

prompt: Fill the blank: what changes between every option in this lesson is one thing — how much of the machine is your ___.
hint: The word the opening video used.

prompt: You take a virtual server. Which of these become yours? Choose all that apply.
hint: The provider’s responsibility ends at the hardware and the network.

choices.text: Security updates
choices.why: Nobody applies them for you, and scanning finds you in hours.

choices.text: Certificates and their renewal
choices.why: Twenty minutes of setup, and then nothing for years.

choices.text: Backups of the database
choices.why: The provider snapshots a disk if asked; nothing backs up your data.

choices.text: The physical hardware failing
choices.why: Theirs, and the one thing they genuinely own.

choices.text: The network between the machine and the internet
choices.why: Also theirs, and also not your morning.

prompt: A site is fast in Brazil and slow in Europe, and the server responds in 40 ms either way. What fixes it?
hint: Two numbers, and only one of them is wrong here.

choices.text: A second database, placed in Europe and kept in step with the first
choices.why: A large undertaking aimed at a number that was already small.

choices.text: A lower TTL on the DNS records, so European resolvers ask more often
choices.why: Asking more often does not shorten the distance to the server.

choices.text: A faster server, since 40 ms is a long time to build a page
choices.why: 40 ms is fine, and it is the same number in both places.

choices.text: A CDN, so European visitors are answered from a copy near them
choices.why: The problem is distance, which is exactly what this addresses.

prompt: The padlock shows on a site sitting behind a CDN. What does it describe?
hint: Two hops, and the browser made one of them.

choices.text: The hop from the browser to the edge
choices.why: What happens behind it is a setting somebody chose.

choices.text: The hop from the edge to the origin, which is the one that carries the data
choices.why: The browser cannot see that hop and its padlock cannot describe it.

choices.text: Neither hop specifically; it records that a certificate exists for the name
choices.why: It records a verified, encrypted connection that the browser itself made.

choices.text: The whole path, from the browser to the origin server
choices.why: The second hop is a separate arrangement and may be plain.

prompt: Put these four in order of how much of the machine is your responsibility, from most to least.
hint: Start with the one where nothing above the hardware is theirs.
items: A platform that runs your code
Functions, called when something needs them
Static files, where nothing runs at all
trap: The tempting order puts static hosting first because it feels the simplest. Simplest to operate is the opposite end: the question is how much is yours, and with files the answer is almost nothing.

prompt: A team is deciding between a fixed monthly server and hourly pricing. Which fact decides it?
hint: Ask what the load looks like over a month.

choices.text: Whether the data has to stay in one country, which fixed pricing guarantees
choices.why: Both arrangements offer a choice of region; neither guarantees it by pricing.

choices.text: Whether the load is steady or spiky
choices.why: A quiet month costs what a busy month costs, and that is good or bad depending.

choices.text: Whether the team knows how to administer a machine, which hourly pricing avoids
choices.why: Hourly pricing at the lowest layer hands you the same machine to administer.

choices.text: Whether the application is written in a language the platform supports
choices.why: A real constraint on one option, and not what separates these two.

prompt: A cached file is served from an edge 8 ms away instead of an origin 200 ms away. How many milliseconds of round-trip latency does that save?
hint: One subtraction.

prompt: What is the honest reason a static site is more reliable than an application server?
hint: The advantages are absences.

choices.text: Static sites receive less traffic, so there is less to go wrong
choices.why: Some of the busiest sites on the internet are files.

choices.text: File servers are written more carefully than application frameworks
choices.why: Both are written carefully; the difference is how much of each is involved.

choices.text: There is no application, no database and no work per request
choices.why: Nothing to crash, nothing to back up, and the file already exists.

choices.text: Static files are replicated by the provider and applications are not
choices.why: Replication is available for both and is not where the difference lies.

prompt: What does this lesson suggest about work that is handed to a provider?
hint: The pattern appears in every reading.

choices.text: It reappears later at a higher price, once you depend on the provider
choices.why: Sometimes true of pricing, and not the point being made.

choices.text: It is replaced by a different, smaller amount of work you can plan for
choices.why: Close, and it understates that the original work is still being done.

choices.text: It disappears, which is what you are paying for
choices.why: It moves, which is a different and more useful thing to believe.

choices.text: It was always there, and the question was whose morning it would be
choices.why: Patching, renewing and backing up exist whoever is doing them.
